t: anyone who kills a person of Israel etc.. There is a prohibition also for killing a gentile, but there is no death penalty for it (see below 2:11).
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verse.
by the sword. By the sword (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:4).
whether he burned him in fire. Even though he does not avenge himself on him in the manner in which he killed.
it is a commandment for the blood avenger. To kill the murderer who was sentenced to death by the court.
and anyone fit to inherit. Anyone who might inherit from the deceased (Chazon Ish, Choshen Mishpat, Sanhedrin 19b; and in the view of Mirkevet HaMishneh, it means one who actually inherits him).
none of the brothers becomes a blood avenger to put their father to death. Although the commandment to be the blood avenger rests on him, he is forbidden to kill his father (see Hilchot Mamrim 5:15).
ransom. Money in place of the punishment.
and you shall not pollute the land, for blood pollutes the land. Do not defile and corrupt the land. Bloodshed damages the land, and only punishing the murderer atones for it.
when he stood and committed the sin for which he is liable to death by the court. When it is already impossible to prevent the act, and the punishment of killing him rests only on the court.
but a pursuer... even at the cost of the pursuer's life. In order to prevent him from murder, it is a commandment to save him even by killing him, even without a court.

they warned him... even though he did not accept the warning. They warn him that if he kills, his punishment is death. And even though the pursuer did not say that he knows and accepts death upon himself if he kills, they kill him (unlike other persons liable to death by the court, who are not put to death if they did not accept a warning, Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:2).
even though he has not yet killed. And has not become liable to death by the court, in any case they kill him to save the one pursued.

as it says, 'you shall cut off her hand, your eye shall not pity'. This verse was said regarding a woman who seizes a man's private parts and endangers him. Ideally one should cut off her hand and not kill her, but if this is not possible, they kill her and do not spare her (see the next halakhah).

both his private parts and anything else that involves danger to life. The same law applies to a woman who seizes a man's private parts as stated in the verse and to other things a person does that involve danger to life.
your eye shall not pity. You shall kill him and not have mercy, in a case where there is no other possibility.
because he is like one pursuing her to kill her. The difficulty of the birth may kill her.
but if once he has put out his head. He is already considered a living child.

for one does not set aside one life for another, and this is the nature of the world. Although he endangers her, he is not considered a true pursuer, since this is the nature of the world and he does not intend to kill her. Therefore her rescue is not to be preferred over his (and although before he put out his head this too is the nature of the world and he is not a true pursuer, since he is also not considered fully alive they permitted killing him by the law of an ordinary pursuer so that she would not be endangered by him).
a betrothed girl. After kiddushin (betrothal) and before marriage.

For just as a man rises up against his fellow and murders him, so is this matter. Pursuing a girl to rape her is equivalent to pursuing a person to kill him; their law is the same, in that in both cases one is commanded to save the victim even at the cost of the pursuer's life.
surely she has a rescuer. From here we learn that whoever is able to save her must do so by any means.
and the same applies to all the other forbidden sexual relations. There is a commandment to prevent rape in these cases, even by taking the life of the rapist.
except for an animal. One may not kill someone pursuing an animal to have relations with it, in order to prevent him from transgressing this prohibition.
the male. The one pursued for homosexual intercourse.
and he began the act, even though he did not complete the intercourse. He inserted only the tip of his organ (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:10).
he is not put to death until he stands trial. Since the transgression has already been committed (see there).

leave him, so that he will not kill me. She fears that when he sees he is being pursued and cannot carry out his scheme, he will kill her. Since she does not consent to being raped and asks to leave him alone only out of fear, we do not listen to her and we kill him (see also Piskei u'Shitot).
as we have explained. Above 5:7.
and he is liable to death, but the court does not put him to death. He is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (Kesef Mishneh).
but the court does not put him to death. Because he was engaged in saving (Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat 425, and see there for another reason).
bandits. Armed robbers.
informers. People who denounce others.
or who knows that a gentile or an oppressor has a complaint against his fellow. That he has a claim and grievance against his fellow and plans to harm him.
and you shall cut off her hand... your eye shall not pity. Said with regard to saving the one pursued (above 5:7).
that lashes are not given for these negative commandments because they involve no action. Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2.
for whoever destroys a single life etc.. See also there 12:3.
with a stone that could kill him. That is capable of killing (below 3:1-2).
or who binds his fellow and leaves him before a lion, and the like. For additional examples see below 3:10-11.

He who sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed - this refers to one who kills by himself. That his law is that he is to be killed by a person ("by man shall his blood be shed"), that is, by a court.
this refers to one who kills himself. Himself.
the expression of seeking is used regarding all three, so their judgment is left to Heaven. God seeks out their life.

if the king of Israel wishes to execute them under royal law and for the betterment of the world. In order to prevent killings, and not under the Torah's penalty for a murderer (see also Hilchot Melachim 3:10).
and so too if the court sees fit to execute etc.. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 24:4.
as a temporary measure. A temporary ruling that will not be established as law for future generations.
if the times require it. In order to prevent other killings.
as they see fit. According to their discretion.
and to imprison them in confinement and distress etc.. In extremely harsh conditions (see further below 4:8).

so that it will not be a stumbling block and a cause of heartache for them etc.. That the killing they committed should not become a stumbling block that leads others' hearts to kill. For if they are not punished, this will cause them to err and think they can kill without being punished for it (see I Samuel 25:31).
exile, if he killed unintentionally. Below, chapter 5.
provided that his months were completed. That he was born after a full nine months of pregnancy, so that he is certainly not a stillborn.
he is considered like a stillborn until he lives thirty days. See also Hilchot Yibbum va'Chalitzah 1:5.

even if one killed a person in the throes of death, he is executed for it. Although he is about to die, he is still considered alive in every respect (Hilchot Avel 4:5), and the one who kills him takes from him whatever life still remains in him.

and if he was dying at the hands of people... the one who kills him, the court does not put him to death. Because the act of killing was not done by him alone; for this reason even those who struck him first and made him a dying person are exempt (below 4:6).

a treifah. A person with a severe defect that will cause death within a short time and who has no cure; he is considered somewhat as dead. In contrast, one in the throes of death is not dying because of a defect or flaw but because of illness or his physical condition.
even though he eats, drinks and walks in the marketplace. He now shows the signs of life of an ordinary person.
cure. Healing.
and from it he will die. From it he will die.
provided that he kills in the presence of the court. And they will execute him on the basis of what they saw, without needing witnesses to testify before them that he killed.

but before witnesses he is exempt, lest the witnesses be proven to be conspiring witnesses etc.. False witnesses whose testimony is disproved receive the punishment they conspired to cause by their testimony, and if they conspired to kill, they themselves are killed. When they testify about a treifah that he is liable to death, even if they are proven to be conspirators they cannot be put to death, for they did not conspire to condemn to death a viable person (Hilchot Edut 20:7). Since they cannot be punished if proven to be conspirators, their testimony is not accepted and no one can be executed on its basis.
one who kills a Canaanite slave is executed for it. As explained in the next halachah.
and if he killed unintentionally, he is exiled. Below 5:3.
a resident alien. A gentile who accepted upon himself not to worship idols and to keep the commandments given to the descendants of Noach (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:7).
he is not executed for it by a court. But if he killed him unintentionally, he is exiled (below 5:3).

for the slave has already accepted commandments and is added to the inheritance of God. For a slave is obligated in the commandments like a woman (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1), and therefore he is not considered a gentile (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:11), and one is liable for killing him as for killing a Jew.

he shall not be avenged, for he is his property. The preceding verse says: "And if a man strikes his slave or his maidservant with a rod and he dies under his hand, he shall surely be avenged" - that is, by the court's death penalty. And in our verse it says: "But if he survives a day or two, he shall not be avenged, for he is his property." From this it follows that if he lived for a full day and did not die immediately, the master is not executed by the court.
a day that is like two days, namely a full twenty-four hours. That twenty-four hours from the time of the blow can include parts of two days.
he is executed for it like any other free person. See below 4:3.
or a fist. Apparently this refers here to a clod of earth (as the Rambam explained this word, see his Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 17:12).
and the like. Destructive implements meant for killing and not for disciplining slaves; a master has no permission to strike his slave with them.
with a rod. A branch or staff.
or a strap. A whip.
and he stipulated with him that he would serve him for thirty days. The owner made a condition with the buyer that after the sale the slave would continue to serve him for thirty days.
because he is not his exclusive property. And the Torah exempted the master who struck his slave only where "he is his property."
who is half slave and half free. A slave who belonged to two partners, one of whom freed him.
or with a stone or with wood. Unlike a stab with iron, which has no minimum measure (below 5:4).

for from a distance of ten his force will be greater. One who throws a stone a distance of ten cubits uses more force than one who throws a stone two cubits, so the strength of the blow from this throw is greater.

for at the greatest distance the force of the blow will diminish. When he throws a stone a very great distance (a hundred cubits), even if he threw it with all his strength, the force of the throw weakens with the distance and the stone does not arrive there with great force.
we assess the wound itself. We examine the manner and severity of the injury.
and so too anything similar. Other factors that could affect the result of the blow.
for his death we assess all its causes. We consider all aspects of the case, whether the blow was capable of killing or whether such a blow does not ordinarily kill.
the Torah gave no minimum measure for an iron implement. See also Hilchot Chovel u'Mazik 1:19.
provided that it has a point like a needle, a skewer, a knife and the like. Implements that pierce and cut the flesh rather than strike it.
with a lump of iron. A mass of raw iron.
he gored him in the head. He butted him.
the force of the blow. Whether it was a strong blow like a kick or a weak one like a push with a finger.
the verse required that the blow be given with hostility. With hatred and in a manner that could kill.
this implies that we assess the force of the blow. Whether it was enough to kill.

and from where do we know that we assess the height of the place? As it says, "and if in hatred he pushes him". That the fall must be from a place suited to killing, from which an enemy pushes someone he wants to kill (Yad Pshutah).

as they said regarding a pit with respect to an animal. That if an animal fell into a pit less than ten handbreadths deep and died, the owner of the pit is exempt from payment, since such a pit is not capable of killing (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 12:10).
pebbles. Small stones.
with a cake of pressed figs. A lump of dried figs.
and it is the weight that kills. Therefore even when he struck with a soft, weak substance, a blow delivered with weight and force can kill.
he pressed down on him in the sea or in the fire. He pushed down on him so that he could not get out.
he is liable even though he was not the one who pushed him in at the start. Since he could have come up out of the water, pressing down on him counts as an act of killing.
one who places his hand over his fellow's mouth and nose. And chokes him.
who bound him and left him in the cold or the heat until he died. In a temperature that cannot be survived, so that he died directly because of being bound there.
who built a structure around him so that air was kept from him. He built a narrow, sealed structure around him until he suffocated from lack of air.
and smoked him out. He introduced smoke there.
who put him in a marble house. A sealed house (see below 5:2).
until the vapor killed him. From lack of oxygen.
and left him in hunger until he died. And so he did not die directly through his binding.

and left him in a place where the cold or heat was due to arrive, and it came and killed him. Since at the time he left him there the temperature there was not one capable of killing, even though it was known that the temperature would change later, this is not considered a direct killing.

who turned a vat over him. He overturned a vessel on him so that he could not get out, and he suffocated inside. However, since while suffocating he shakes the vat and a little air gets in, he is not liable. And above in halachah 9, where he built a structure around him, it speaks of a case where no air entered at all, so he is liable (Or Sameach; and see Kesef Mishneh, Mirkevet ha-Mishneh, Even ha-Ezel and other commentators, who resolved it in other ways).
who removed the roof from over him. He removed the roof from the place where he was staying, and he died of cold.
who made a snake bite him. He pressed the snake's teeth against him, and the snake bit him and he died.
and needless to say if he set a dog or a snake on him. He signaled to it with his hand or with his voice to attack him. Since in these cases the animal killed and he only caused it, he is exempt.
he is a murderer, and "the One who seeks out blood" seeks blood from him. Even though he did not kill directly and cannot be executed by a court, he is considered a murderer and God will punish him.
a shield. A protective cover.
neither of them is executed by a court. The act of the first was not one capable of killing, and the second only caused a killing and there was no actual act of killing.
and blood is demanded from him. He is punished by Heaven.
who play with a ball. They throw a heavy ball with great force against a wall, and the ball killed on its return.

within four cubits they are exempt. The thrower intends the ball to return a long distance from the wall, so when the ball killed within the four cubits nearest the wall, the thrower's intention was not fulfilled and he is exempt (Ran, Sanhedrin 77b). Some write that within the first four cubits next to the wall the ball returns from the force of the collision with the wall and not from the thrower's force, and therefore he is exempt (Meiri, there).
provided that it was capable of killing, as we have explained. Above, halachot 1-3.

if he threw a stone upward and it veered sideways and killed, he is liable. Although the stone killed as it fell and not by the force of his throw, since it fell to the side and did not return to the place from which it was thrown, this fall is considered a throw that came from his force. But if the stone fell straight down and killed as it fell, he is exempt (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 77b-78a).
provided that he dies from the first force that came from his actions. That he dies from the first surge of water that arrived directly because of the flooding he caused.

and from monetary payments. Ordinarily a murderer is not liable for payments for the person he killed, since he is punished with the death penalty, and even in a case where he is exempt from death he is exempt from payments (see Hilchot Chovel 4:5; however, if he did not intend to kill at all but to strike this one and struck his fellow, even though he killed him he is liable for payments, there, halachah 6).
for the cities of refuge do not receive him, as will be explained. Below 6:10.
therefore one who throws a stone into a group of Israelites and kills one of them is exempt. Since he did not intend to kill this particular victim.
and the stone went and landed on his heart, and it was capable of killing on his heart, and he died... he is exempt. Since he intended to strike in a way that was not capable of killing.

he intended to strike him on his heart... and it went and landed on his loins, and it was not capable of killing on his loins, and he died, he is exempt. Although he intended to kill in a way that is capable of killing, since in fact he killed in a way that is not capable, he is exempt.
and he is not exiled, for one who kills intentionally is not exiled. Only one who kills unintentionally is exiled.
we assess him. Whether he is likely to die from the blow.
he pays five things and is released. He pays the five payments that a person who injures his fellow pays: damages, pain, healing, loss of time, and shame (Hilchot Chovel 1:1).

even if the injured person became ill, grew worse and died from the blow, he is exempt. Since at first they exempted him from death, they do not reverse themselves (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 78b).
and if he improved. The illness.
the one who struck pays five things and is released. And in this case, since he recovered fully, even if he died afterward the striker is exempt from death and liable for payments.

this is what the Torah says: "upon his staff". The verse says: "If he gets up and walks outside upon his staff, the one who struck him is cleared; only he shall pay for his lost time and fully heal him." From this it follows that when the injured person walks on his staff, the striker is exempted from death and made liable for money.

that he walks on the staff of his own strength. That he relies on his own strength alone, like a healthy person. For until he fully recovers, even if his condition improves the striker is not to be released, because if the injured person dies the striker will be liable to death (as explained in the next halachah).
and he improved from what he had been. But did not recover fully.

we do not make a second assessment once he has improved. After he has improved from his illness we do not examine again whether he is likely to die from his condition. Even if he reached stages of recovery that took him out of danger, if his condition later worsens and he dies, the striker is liable to death.
for there is a basis for the matter. According to the first assessment there is a basis to say that he died from the blow, and the change in his condition does not cancel that assessment.
ten people struck him with ten sticks and he died. All of them caused his death.
for many people were sitting and an arrow came out from among them and killed. All of them shot the arrow together (Shelal David, Yad Pshutah).
and one threw a stone last, and it was capable of killing, and he died, this last one is executed for it. For although the earlier ones injured him, he alone killed him.
whose verdict had been completed. They had sentenced him to death in court.
all of them are exempt from death. For we do not know who the one is whose verdict was not completed, and there is no way to complete his verdict.
for a person's verdict is completed only in his presence. Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:7.
and they imprison all of them. For all of them are murderers, and since they cannot be executed they are imprisoned in the manner explained in the next halachah (Aruch ha-Shulchan, section 34).
and the two witnesses did not see him together etc.. Therefore their testimony does not combine and no one can be judged on its basis (Hilchot Edut 4:1).

or who killed before two witnesses without warning. One who commits a transgression that carries the death penalty is not executed by a court unless he was warned ("hatra'ah") before the act that this act carries the death penalty (Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:2). In a case of murder without warning, although there are witnesses and he is certainly the murderer, he is not executed by a court.

whose witnesses were contradicted in the examinations but not contradicted in the interrogations. The witnesses were found truthful on the essence of their testimony, but contradictions were found in peripheral matters related to their testimony (see Hilchot Edut 1:5-6), and therefore the murderer cannot be sentenced to death.
they put them into a cell. They place them in a dungeon.
and feed them meager bread and scanty water. A limited amount of food and drink (based on Isaiah 30:20).
only he was not like Achav. He was not a wicked king like him.

no sin was found in him that would condemn him to destruction, and there was nothing else to outweigh it. Against all his other sins, merits were found that saved him from destruction (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 102b).

as it says, "and a spirit went out and stood before God" - this is the spirit of Navot etc.. Navot's spirit received permission to mislead four hundred prophets ("you will entice him and also prevail") and cause them to prophesy falsely that Achav would defeat Aram, and because of them he went out to war and died there.

and this wicked man did not kill with his own hand but only caused it. Izevel sent a letter in Achav's name to the residents of Navot's city to falsely accuse him with false testimony and put him to death (see I Kings, chapter 21).
the heretics, who are Jews who worship idols. See also Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7.
or one who commits transgressions to spite. See also there 5:9 (there they are called "apostates," but here they are included in the general term "heretic").
and the epicureans, who deny the Torah and prophecy. See there 5:8.
it is a commandment to kill them if one has the power to kill them. Because they are enemies of Israel and lead the people away from God (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:1).
he first removes the ladder. He removes the ladder beforehand, before the person climbs up.

and Jewish shepherds of small livestock. It is forbidden to raise small livestock in the Land of Israel because they damage the fields of others (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:2). The case here is where this is rampant (see the next halachah).
who does not persist in his wickedness constantly but commits transgressions for his own enjoyment. Occasionally, on a casual basis.
out of appetite. Due to his desire and not in rebellion.
and it is forbidden to stand idly by his blood. It is forbidden to stand aside if he is about to die and one is able to save him (see above 1:14).
from a city. A town.

to the cities of refuge. Cities designated to receive those who kill unintentionally (below chapter 8). The killer stays in the city of refuge until the death of the High Priest, and staying there protects him from the blood avenger.
and the court was warned not to take a ransom from one who killed unintentionally. For the law of a similar case regarding an intentional killer, see above 1:4.

and you shall not take a ransom for one who flees to his city of refuge. The continuation of the verse is: "to return to dwell in the land until the death of the priest." This means that it is forbidden to take a ransom from one whose law is to flee to a city of refuge, or who has already fled, so that he may live in his own city and not in the city of refuge before the death of the High Priest.
even though they assessed him as likely to die, and he became ill and died. And if this blow had been intentional, he would have been liable to death (above 4:3).
perhaps he hastened his own death. By thrashing and flailing, he prevented the blood from clotting and sealing the injured blood vessels, and as a result lost a great deal of blood.
the air entered his wound. And infected his wound, and he died from the infection.
both of the two signs. The signs of slaughter, the windpipe and the esophagus, and he will certainly die.
and he stood for a short while. He remained alive for a short time before he died.
he is not exiled for him. Perhaps there was another factor that hastened his death.
the slave. A Canaanite slave, for whose intentional killing one is liable to death (above 2:10).
a resident alien. Even though one is not liable to death for killing him intentionally (there, halachah 11), nevertheless one is exiled for killing him unintentionally.

even though he acted unintentionally, he is executed, for a person is always forewarned. We hold the killer liable even when he killed unintentionally, just as a person who causes damage is liable in monetary law in every case, whether intentional or unintentional (Hilchot Chovel 1:11). Since a gentile can be punished even without warning, he can be executed even when he killed unintentionally (Kesef Mishneh).
this is close to intentional, and he is executed for it. Because he should have learned that killing is forbidden (Hilchot Melachim 10:1; for the law of a Jew who killed in this way, see below 6:10).
and a gentile who killed a gentile unintentionally, the cities of refuge do not receive him. Therefore the blood avenger may kill him, but the gentile courts may not kill him (Hilchot Melachim 10:1).
another trade that he does not need. For his livelihood.
but if he disciplines his son in order to teach him Torah... he is exempt. Since these blows involve a mitzvah, one is exempt for them, as explained in the next halachah.
as it says, "to chop wood" - this refers to optional matters. An act similar to chopping wood, which is an act that involves no mitzvah.
initially, whether he killed unintentionally or intentionally, they send him ahead to the cities of refuge. Immediately after the killing, the killer flees to a city of refuge.
one who is released, they release him. For example, one who killed unintentionally in a manner close to an accident (below 6:3).
they assign him two Torah scholars etc.. To appease the blood avenger if he wishes to kill him on the way, and to inform him that he may not kill him since the killing was unintentional.

and they say to them. The Torah scholars say to the blood avengers (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 2:8), and perhaps here it should be explained that they say this to the people of the city of refuge (see Meiri, Makkot 10b).

if the blood avenger killed one who killed unintentionally outside the boundary of his city of refuge, he is exempt. On the way to a city of refuge (when he flees there after killing and when he returns there after being sentenced), the blood avenger is forbidden to kill him, but if he did kill him he is exempt from death.

and he left its boundary intentionally, he has made himself liable to death. Since he had already reached the city of refuge, he is forbidden to leave it, and if he leaves, the blood avenger may kill him, and others are forbidden to kill him but are exempt from death if they killed him.
outside its boundary. The open areas and fields around the city receive the killer like the city itself (below 8:11).

if he left the boundary of his city of refuge unintentionally, anyone who kills him... is exiled for it. Since he left unintentionally, his blood was not permitted, so the one who kills him has the law of one who kills unintentionally and is liable to exile. The Rambam's words imply that even one who kills him intentionally is exiled (see Aruch ha-Shulchan 425:42), and the commentators asked why he would be exiled (see Tiferet Yisrael, Makkot 2:7, Lashad ha-Shemen and others). Some write that here it speaks of a case where he killed him unintentionally (Arukh la-Ner, Makkot 12a, Minchat Chinuch 410; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 2:7, who wrote that if he killed him intentionally he is to be executed).
the altar receives. It has the law of a city of refuge.
only the top of the altar of the Eternal House. The top of the altar in the Temple, which was sanctified forever, but the altar that was in the Tabernacle did not receive.
while he has service in his hand. While he is performing the service.
a non-priest. One who is not a kohen.
or a kohen who is not performing service at the time he was killed. At the time the blood avenger killed him.
holding its horns. Holding the corners of the altar that are raised above the top of the altar.
they assign him guards. To protect him on the way from the blood avenger.
one liable to exile. Because he killed unintentionally.

who feared the king, that he would execute him by royal law. For example, one who rebelled against the king (see Hilchot Melachim 3:8) or who killed in a way that does not carry the death penalty in court and the king is obligated to execute him under royal law (above 2:4).

from the court, that they would execute him as a temporary measure. For when the court sees a need, they may as a temporary measure execute a murderer who is not liable to death in court (there) and other offenders who violate their words (Hilchot Sanhedrin 24:4).
and he fled to the altar and leaned against it. Even if he did not stand on its top.
kills unintentionally with complete inadvertence. That he could not have taken care to prevent the killing.
and his law is that he is exiled to the cities of refuge and is protected, as we have explained. Above 5:1.

and his law is that he is exempt from exile, and if the blood avenger killed him, he is executed for it. Since it is close to an accident, he does not have the law of one who killed unintentionally and he is entirely exempt from exile, so the blood avenger is forbidden to kill him. And if the blood avenger killed him intentionally, he is liable to death.

because his sin is grave, exile does not atone for him and the cities of refuge do not receive him. Exile receives one who killed unintentionally and protects him from the blood avenger, and staying there atones for his act. When an unintentional act is close to intentional, because of the gravity of the sin exile does not atone, and staying there does not protect him.
if the blood avenger found him anywhere and killed him, he is exempt. Even inside a city of refuge.
and what should he do? He should sit and guard himself from the blood avenger. This killer has no protection from the blood avenger, and he must always take care and flee from him.

who killed him on the testimony of a single witness. Although a single witness is not believed so as to permit the killer's blood, in a case where the blood avenger killed him on his own judgment, he cannot be punished (Migdal Oz; and some write that this speaks of a special testimony that must be believed but cannot be used to execute, as above 4:8 - Kesef Mishneh, Radbaz and others).

one who throws a stone into the public domain and kills... whether he demolished it by day or by night. Since people are found in the public domain day and night, the thrower or demolisher must check at all times that no people are there, and if he did not check, he is negligent.
he demolished it into a garbage heap. He demolished his wall into a garbage dump.
made for people to relieve themselves there at night. People go there to relieve themselves at night.
and a person happened by and sat there. A person happened to be there during the day, which is a time when people ordinarily do not relieve themselves there.

and a stone fell on him at the time of the demolition and he died, he is exiled. Since this is a time when people are not found there, he is not negligent, but since people sometimes happen to be there, he is not blameless, and therefore he is exiled (Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 8a).

"and he finds his fellow" - excluding one who puts himself in the way. The verse obligates exile where the killer threw something and it found the victim, but where the victim brought himself into the range of the thrown object, the thrower is exempt from exile.

as it says, "and he was not his enemy" etc.. The verse says that the killer who is exiled is not an "enemy" of the victim, since a person who hates is presumed to have killed in a manner close to intentional.
he is presumed to be close to intentional. And the king has permission to execute him as the times require, like other murderers who cannot be tried (Hilchot Melachim 3:10).

and similarly if he entered a corner and killed him there unintentionally. The killer collided with the victim who came from the side at a crossing of paths, and since it is impossible to see whether there is someone around the corner, he should have been careful when entering there, and if he was not careful, he is negligent.
who intended to throw two and threw four. He intended to throw a distance of two cubits and in fact threw a distance of four cubits.
or who intended to kill this one and killed that one. In this case he is exempt from death even though he acted intentionally (above 4:1).
a splinter. A piece of wood that splits off from chopping wood in a carpentry shop.

for this is like an accident, since it is not something likely to happen in most cases but is a wonder. Falling while going up is not common and is in the category of an accident. But falling while coming down is common and one must be careful of it, and if he was not careful and killed, he is exiled, as explained in the next section.
and he fell on his fellow and killed him. The person himself fell.
he was rolling with a roller. Smoothing the clay on the roof with a cylindrical stone fitted with handles to move it back and forth.

a butcher who was chopping and raised his hand etc.. To cut the meat, the butcher brings the knife down with great force. At first he raises the knife as high as possible and then lowers it a little behind him to increase the momentum of the blow; this stage is considered "the way of going up," and even if he killed while lowering the knife downward behind him, he is not exiled. After the butcher swung the knife backward, he brings it down on the meat: at first he raises the knife from behind him upward and then brings it down with momentum in front of him; this whole stage is considered "the way of going down," and even if he killed while raising the knife upward, he is exiled.
with a cleaver. An ax used for cutting meat.
even in a descent that is for the sake of an ascent. For example, if he lowers the cleaver behind him when raising it upward, or when climbing a ladder, as explained in the next halachah.

he was going up a ladder and a rung slipped out from under his foot and fell and killed, he is exempt from exile. Although when he stepped on the rung of the ladder he pressed it down with his feet, since this descent is for the purpose of his ascent, he is not exiled.
and similarly one who intended to throw to this side etc.. Here additional cases of unintentional killing close to an accident are mentioned.

when a stone was placed in his lap and he never noticed it. Since he was never aware of this stone, he did not need to be careful, and he is considered as having been prevented by circumstances beyond his control when it fell and killed.
the iron slipped from its handle. The iron head of the ax slipped from the handle as he swung it.
the iron slipped from the wood being split. While he was striking the wood, the iron slipped off because of a piece of wood that struck it and knocked it out of the handle.
as it says, "and he shall live". Fleeing to the city of refuge is to give the exile life, and one must support the exile's life in the city of refuge.
and similarly a teacher who was exiled, his yeshiva is exiled with him. So that he will have life from the Torah that he teaches.

a slave who was exiled to a city of refuge, his master is not obligated to feed him, and the work of his hands belongs to his master. A master is not obligated to provide food for his Canaanite slave, and even if he does not provide him food, the slave must continue to work for him and live on charity (Hilchot Avadim 9:7); and even in a city of refuge, of which it says "and he shall live," the master is not obligated to provide food for his slave (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 12a).

a woman who was exiled to a city of refuge, her husband is obligated to support her etc.. The Sages instituted that a husband supports his wife and in return the work of her hands belongs to him, and they established that the husband may not say to his wife to take the work of her hands for herself and he will not support her, lest the work of her hands not suffice for her food expenses (Hilchot Ishut 12:4); however, if the work of her hands suffices for her, he may tell her to support herself from the work of her hands. The same applies to a woman who was exiled to a city of refuge: he is obligated to support her and cannot say to her, "I will not support you and I will not take the work of your hands."
and at the time the High Priest dies. The death of the High Priest releases the exile from exile, and after it his body may also be taken out of the city.

the Levites who dwell in the cities of refuge. Besides these cities being cities of refuge for unintentional killers, they were given to the Levites at the time the land was divided so that they would live in them.

when one of them dies, he is not buried in the city. Although killers are buried there temporarily, it is forbidden for the Levites to bury their dead in their cities or in their boundary (see Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 13:3).
and he does not leave the city. He did not flee from this city to another city of refuge, since he is forbidden to leave the city because of the first killing.
and a Levite who killed in his own city is exiled to another city of the Levite cities. He must leave there, since for him it is a place of residence and not a city of refuge.
because all of them receive, as will be explained. All the cities of the Levites serve as cities of refuge (below 8:9).
and if he killed outside the Levite cities and fled to his own city, it receives him. The city receives him, even though before the killing this city served as his residence.

"and he shall speak in the ears of the elders of that city his words" etc.. The verse speaks of a killer who was exiled to a city of refuge and stands before the elders of the city and tells them that he killed unintentionally. The verse requires that his words be words specific to him, and not words similar to what was said by most of the people of the city.
elders. Judges.
he says to them, "I am a killer". And I am not worthy of honor.
the exile never leaves his city of refuge etc.. By virtue of his sentence of exile to a city of refuge, he cannot leave even temporarily (see Yad Pshutah).
from the hand of the troop. Enemy soldiers.
from the hand of the river. Rescuing one who is drowning.
and from a collapse. To extricate a person from under it.
like Yoav ben Tzeruyah. Who was the commander of the army.
and if he left, he made himself liable to death, as we have explained. Above 5:10.

whether a High Priest anointed with the anointing oil or one who is dressed in the additional garments. A High Priest is appointed by being anointed with the anointing oil. In a time when there is no anointing oil, the appointment is made by wearing the eight garments of the High Priest (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:12). One who killed unintentionally leaves the city of refuge and ends his exile at the death of the High Priest, whether he was anointed with the anointing oil or appointed by wearing the garments special to the High Priest.

and whether a High Priest who is serving or a priest who was replaced. When a High Priest is removed from his position (because of a blemish, impurity and the like), although he does not actually serve as High Priest, the laws of a High Priest still apply to him (Hilchot Shegagot 15:7), and therefore at his death the killer leaves the city of refuge.
the priest anointed for war. A kohen appointed to speak to the people when they go out to war, who is anointed with the anointing oil (Hilchot Melachim 7:1).

he does not bring back, because he is like an ordinary priest. Although he was anointed with the anointing oil, he is considered an ordinary priest and serves in the Temple in four garments like the other priests (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:21), and therefore his death does not return the killer from his exile.
and there was no other High Priest there. At the time their verdict was completed.
these are exiled and never leave the city of refuge. For a killer leaves the city of refuge only at the death of a High Priest who was High Priest at the time his verdict was completed.
he is exempt from exile. Since his verdict of exile was completed, the death of the High Priest exempts him, even though he had not yet actually gone into exile.

and the High Priest was found to be the son of a divorced woman or of a chalutzah etc.. It became clear that the High Priest who served at the time of his verdict was not a kohen but a chalal. Since there was no other High Priest then, his law is that of a killer whose verdict was completed without a High Priest.
son of a divorced woman. His father is a kohen and his mother a divorcee; a divorcee is forbidden to a kohen, and her child from him is a chalal (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:3).

chalutzah. A yevamah from whom the yavam performed chalitzah so that she could marry another is forbidden to a kohen by rabbinic law, and her child from a kohen is a chalal (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:8).
for a position of authority. A public appointment.

although one who wounds his father intentionally is liable to the court's death penalty like one who kills any other person. One who wounds his father or mother and injures them intentionally is liable to death, and his death is by strangulation (Hilchot Mamrim 5:5).
as we have explained. Above 5:1.

Moshe Rabbeinu set apart three on the other side of the Jordan. On the eastern side of the Jordan, the land of Sichon and Og: Betzer in the portion of Reuven, Ramot in the portion of Gad, and Golan in the portion of half the tribe of Menasheh (Deuteronomy 4:43).

and Yehoshua set apart three in the land of Canaan. On the western side of the Jordan: Kedesh in the Galilee in the portion of Naftali, Shechem in the portion of Efraim, and Chevron in the portion of Yehudah (Joshua 20:7).

in the cities of the Kenite, the Kenizzite and the Kadmonite, with which a covenant was made with Avraham Avinu and which had not yet been conquered. In the Covenant between the Parts, God promised Avraham Avinu the lands of ten nations (Genesis 15:18-21). Israel conquered the seven lands of the Canaanite nations when they entered the land, and the remaining three lands they are destined to conquer in the days of the King Mashiach.
to prepare the roads to the cities of refuge. To prepare roads that lead directly to the cities of refuge.
hill. A mound.
valley. A ravine.
no less than thirty-two cubits. Double the minimum width of a public thoroughfare (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 100b).
and "Refuge, refuge" was written at the crossroads. At a place where the road splits, they would put up signs to direct the killer so that he would know to flee to the city of refuge.
on the fifteenth of Adar every year the court sends out emissaries to repair the roads. After the rainy season, when the roads are damaged (Rav Ovadiah, Shekalim 1:1).
and a court that was negligent in this matter, the verse considers it as if they shed blood. For if the killer is delayed on the road, the blood avenger might overtake him and kill him.
they measure between each of the cities of refuge. They measure the distance between the cities.
at the beginning of their designation. Before they are set apart.
until they are divided into equal thirds. So that the distance between one city and the next is equal.
not small towns. Where food is not readily available, and the killer would be forced to leave the city to obtain food (Rashi, Makkot 10a).
and not large metropolises. Where there are many people and the blood avenger could mingle among them and kill the killer (there).
and they settle them only in a place of markets and a place of water. So that sources of livelihood will be available in them.

and they settle them only in a place of dense population. So that there will be additional cities around the city (there; and Meiri explained that "dense population" refers to soldiers who protect the city).
its residents diminished. The residents of the city decreased and it became a small town.
priests, Levites and Israelites. So that every type of exile will find people there whose outlook is close to his own (Arukh la-Ner, there; and see Ritva, there, who explained differently).
traps. Snares.
and they do not spin ropes in them. They do not twist and manufacture ropes in them.

so that the foot of the blood avenger will not frequent there. Setting traps and spinning ropes require a large space, and not everywhere is it possible to set aside space for this; therefore, in a city where there is a large space, people from all the surroundings come for these purposes, and the blood avenger could also come there (Arukh la-Ner, there; and see Meiri, there, who explained differently).

all the Levite cities receive. The Levites did not receive a portion in the land but received forty-eight cities within the portions of the tribes. The six cities of refuge were among the cities given to the Levites, but not only they served as cities of refuge; rather, all the Levite cities receive like cities of refuge.

the six cities of refuge receive whether knowingly or unknowingly etc.. A killer who enters one of the six cities of refuge, even if he did not know it is a city of refuge and did not intend to enter it to protect himself from the blood avenger, is received, and if the blood avenger killed him he is liable to death. But in the other Levite cities, the killer must enter them with the intention that they serve as a city of refuge for him.
and a killer who lives in the cities of refuge does not pay rent for his house. Since the Torah designated the city for killers, he is entitled to free housing.
any city that receives, its boundary receives like it. Three thousand cubits outside the city on every side (Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 13:2, and see Piskei u'Shitot there).
a tree standing within the boundary. Its trunk is within the boundary of the city.
and its branches. Its boughs.

once he reaches under the branches he is received... once he reaches its root he is received. The part that extends outside the boundary (whether it is the branches or the root) is drawn after the part within the boundary, and from the moment he is there he is received.
they leave it in its place. And do not bury it (see below 9:2).
five elders of the Great Court in Jerusalem. Judges from the Great Sanhedrin that sits in the Temple and has seventy-one judges (see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:1, 5:5).
and they measure from it to the cities surrounding the slain person. To determine which city is nearest and must bring the calf.

even if he was found next to this city, where it is known for certain that it is the nearest, there is a commandment to measure. As for the reason for this, the Rambam wrote in the Guide for the Perplexed (3:40) that perhaps through the activity of measuring and the publicity it generates, the killer will be found.
they bury the slain person in his place. In the place where he was found (see below 9:9).
from the property of the people of that city. From their funds.
a stream that flows forcefully. With a strong current.
and they break its neck there with a cleaver from behind. They cut off its head from the back (from the nape) with an ax used for cutting meat.
the elders of the city. The judges.
and we did not send him away without food. We did not send him off without provisions for the journey.
without escort. Without accompanying him as he set out on the road (see Hilchot Avel 14:3).
and we do not estimate it. We do not measure the ground by approximation but exactly (unlike the measurement of the Shabbat boundary, see Hilchot Shabbat 28:15-16).
a court of twenty-three. Authorized to judge capital cases.

Jerusalem does not bring a broken-necked calf, because it was not divided among the tribes. When the Land of Israel was divided among the various tribes, Jerusalem was not divided, and it remained the property of the whole people (see also Hilchot Beit ha-Bechirah 7:14).

they leave it and measure to the other nearby towns. Although one cannot measure to the nearest city, the law of the broken-necked calf is not canceled; rather, they measure to the other cities and the second nearest city brings it.
he was found near the border. Near the boundary of the province.
we follow the majority, and the larger city brings the calf. For it is reasonable that the killer came from the people of the more populous city, even if it is farther away.
although we follow the majority by Torah law. In many laws doubts are resolved according to the majority (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 8:11, Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 17:7-8 and others).

and we follow the nearest. Similar to the law of the broken-necked calf, in other cases doubt is resolved by distance, such as consecrated shekels that were found and it is not known from where they fell (Hilchot Shekalim 3:14-15), and a stolen dove whose dovecote is unknown (Hilchot Gezelah 15:18).
the majority takes precedence. Even in cases where we follow the nearest, if there is a majority in a more distant place we follow it (see there).
exactly between two towns. Placed precisely in the middle of the distance between them.
because it is impossible to be exact. It is impossible to measure with complete precision, and surely the slain person is closer to one of the towns than the other.
even by human hands. Even in a measurement done by people, it is impossible to be completely precise.
from his nose. From his nose.
they bring the body to the head. This law applies to the place of burial regardless of the place of measurement (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 45b).

and they bury him in his place... and so too any met mitzvah. This slain person, and likewise any person lying on the road who has no one to bury him (a "met mitzvah," Hilchot Avel 3:8), is entitled to be buried where he was found, unless he was found inside a city or on a road between fields in a place where burial is impossible (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:3).

they measure from the nose of each one of them etc.. They measure from each slain person separately, and if they are close to different cities, each city must bring a calf for the dead person near it. But if all the slain are close to the same city, it brings one calf for all of them.
they measure from the uppermost as they lie. Even if the nose of the lower one is not beneath the nose of the upper one.
a slain person, not a strangled one. Only if he was killed by stabbing with a sword and the like is he called "slain" (Rashi, Sotah 45b, and see Malbim on Deuteronomy 21:1).
twitching. Writhing before the end of his death.
on the ground. In an exposed place.
hidden in a heap. Concealed in a pile of stones.
fallen. Lying on the ground.

even if one witness saw the killer, even a slave etc.. Although ordinarily only two valid witnesses are believed to testify, in the case of the broken-necked calf one witness is believed, even if he is disqualified (Hilchot Edut 5:1-3).
a slave or a woman. Who are disqualified from testifying (there 9:1).
disqualified to testify because of a transgression. One who is disqualified from testifying because of transgressions he committed (there, chapter 10).
therefore, once murderers multiplied openly, the broken-necked calf was abolished. For there is a concern that a single witness saw the killer (Tiferet Yisrael, Sotah 9:9).

one witness says, "I saw the killer," and one witness contradicts him... they break the neck. Since they contradict each other, their testimony is void and there is no testimony about the killing, so they break the neck.

he is believed like two for this purpose etc.. For the purpose of the testimony of the broken-necked calf, a single witness is believed and counts as two witnesses, and after his testimony is accepted, a single witness cannot contradict him (for a similar law see Hilchot Sotah 1:16).

they are like two testimonies that contradict each other, and they break the neck. The single witness is believed as two, and since the testimonies cancel each other there is no testimony about the slain person, and the neck is to be broken (for a similar law see Hilchot Sotah 1:17).

whether both came together or one after the other. Although the woman's testimony is accepted, it is not considered full testimony of two witnesses. Therefore even if she was contradicted after her testimony was accepted, her testimony is void (and the same applies to the testimony of other disqualified witnesses, Migdal Oz).

two say "we saw," and one says to them "you did not see," they do not break the neck. Even in the testimony of the broken-necked calf, the testimony of one witness does not cancel the testimony of two, even when they came to testify together.

but if one witness said "I saw the killer," and two women or two disqualified witnesses say to him "you did not see," they do not break the neck. In the testimony of the broken-necked calf, the one valid witness counts as two, and all the women or disqualified witnesses together count as one witness (as explained in the next halachah). Therefore when disqualified witnesses contradict one valid witness, his testimony stands and they do not break the neck. This speaks of a case where the women or disqualified witnesses came after the testimony of the valid witness was accepted; but if they came together, the testimony of the women or disqualified witnesses is considered equal to the testimony of the witness, and the testimonies cancel each other and they break the neck (Mirkevet ha-Mishneh, Lechem Yehudah, Even ha-Ezel, and see Hilchot Sotah 1:18; and the Raavad understood that in the Rambam's view even when they came together, two women do not contradict one valid witness, and therefore he objected).

two women or two disqualified witnesses say "we saw the killer," and one witness contradicts them and says "you did not see," they break the neck. The testimony of several disqualified witnesses is considered the testimony of one valid witness, so their testimonies cancel each other and they break the neck.

this is the rule for disqualified witnesses: follow the majority in every place. We follow the majority of those testifying, and therefore in the opposite case, when four say "we saw" and three say "you did not see," they do not break the neck (for this principle see also Hilchot Sotah 1:19).
on the other side of the Jordan. On the eastern side of the Jordan, the land of Sichon and Og, the portion of Reuven, Gad and half of Menasheh.
two years old or less. In its first or second year.

blemishes do not disqualify it, but nevertheless if it was a treifah it is disqualified etc.. The broken-necked calf is not a sacrificial animal, but at the same time its bringing is meant to atone for the blood of the slain person and the language of atonement is used regarding it (Deuteronomy 21:8). Therefore, unlike a sacrificial animal, which is disqualified if it has a blemish, a blemish does not disqualify the calf. However, if it is a treifah it is disqualified like a sacrificial animal.
treifah. Having a wound or defect because of which it is likely to die (for the details of treifot see Hilchot Shechitah chapters 5-10).

all work disqualifies the calf, as it disqualifies a red heifer. The calf whose neck is broken and the red heifer, whose ashes are used to purify from corpse impurity, are valid only if no work of any kind was done with them (see Hilchot Para 1:7).

for the yoke disqualifies, whether at the time of work or not at the time of work. The yoke is a bar placed on the animal's neck by which it pulls a plow or cart attached behind the yoke. When a yoke has been tied on it, it is disqualified even if it did not plow (there).

and other types of work disqualify only at the time of work. For example, if she was brought in to thresh in a place where animals thresh the grain, she is not disqualified unless she actually threshes (there).
to carry it. That the calf carry the cloak.
and similarly anything of this kind, as we explained in Hilchot Parah Adumah. 1:7.
because it is described with the term atonement, like sacrifices. And the slaughter of sacrifices is done only by day (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 4:1).
for mitzvot are not performed in bundles. See also Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:6, Hilchot Avadim 3:9.
and it is buried in the place where its neck was broken. See also Hilchot Pesulei ha-Mukdashin 19:11.
if it died or was slaughtered after it went down, it is forbidden for benefit. Although in the end its neck was not broken, since it went down to the stream it is forbidden for benefit.
its witnesses were found to be conspiring witnesses. It became clear that the witnesses on whose word the calf's neck was to be broken were false witnesses.

it is permitted for benefit. For it became clear retroactively that they were not obligated to bring a calf at all, so in this case going down to the stream does not make the calf forbidden for benefit.

if the killer was found before the calf's neck was broken, it goes out and grazes with the herd. Finding the killer cancels the obligation to bring the calf, so even if he was found after the calf went down to the stream, the calf is permitted for benefit and may return to the herd. Even if it already went down to the stream and became forbidden for benefit, when the slain person's killer was found it became clear that its consecration was made in error and it is permitted retroactively (Meiri, Kiddushin 57a; Kesef Mishneh).

for it comes from the beginning on account of the uncertainty; its atonement was for the uncertainty, and it is gone. The reason the calf's neck is broken is that it is not known who the killer is. Therefore, if at the time the calf's neck was broken the killer was still unknown, the calf atoned for the uncertainty and lack of knowledge at that time and the laws of a broken-necked calf apply to it, and even if the killer is found afterward, the laws of a broken-necked calf remain on it (burial in its place, prohibition of benefit).

and even though the murderer was found after its neck was broken, he is put to death. Like other murderers. For although the breaking of the neck atones for the people of the city, it does not atone for the murderer himself.
and to quarry stones there. To hew.

those obligated to bring a broken-necked calf over whom Yom Kippur passed are obligated to bring it after Yom Kippur. Their law is not that of one who is uncertain whether he sinned and is obligated to bring an asham talui, for Yom Kippur atones for his uncertainty (Hilchot Shegagot 3:9).
It is a positive commandment for a person to make a parapet for his roof. In a rented house this mitzvah rests on the tenant and not on the landlord (Hilchot Sechirut 6:3).
a dwelling house. One used for living.
a storehouse. A warehouse.
and a cattle shed. A barn.
any house that does not measure four cubits by four cubits is exempt from a parapet. For a similar law regarding mezuzah, see Hilchot Mezuzah 6:2.
if so, why does it say "your roof". In the singular, from which one can conclude that there is no obligation in a house owned by partners.
if the public domain is higher than his roof, he does not need a parapet. To prevent falling from the public domain into his property.
the height of the parapet. Above the edge of the roof.
no less than ten handbreadths, so that one who falls will not fall from it. A low parapet does not prevent falling and does not fulfill its purpose.
and lashes are not given for this negative commandment because it involves no action. For lashes are given for a transgression only if it involves an actual act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2).
a fence. A raised stone wall around a pit.
as it says, "Beware and guard your life". From this we learn that there is an obligation to guard one's life against danger.
"I am endangering myself, and what concern is it of others?" etc.. Even though he thinks that his endangering himself is no one else's business, he is given rabbinic lashes for it.

a person should not put his mouth to a pipe gushing water and drink. He should not press his mouth to the end of the pipe and drink directly from it in a way that he does not see the water before drinking it.
lest a snake have drunk from them. And injected venom into them.
mixed wine. Mixed with water.
and the brine. The sauce that is extracted from fish.
and similarly anything like these. Moist cut and crushed fruits and vegetables.
as long as steam rises from them. That vapors rise from them.
provided that it is flowing and descending. Dripping continuously without interruption.
pickling water. Water in which a fruit or vegetable was pickled.
and boiled-vegetable water. Water in which a fruit or vegetable was cooked.
and lupine water. Water in which lupines were pickled or cooked (a kind of legume that is cooked several times).
water in which he soaked pickled things, boiled things and lupines. In which he soaked the foods but did not cook them.
if their taste changed, they are not subject to the uncovered-liquids prohibition. That their law becomes that of pickling water.
quinces. Hazarolim.
and damsons. Plums.

for a sick person. For the purpose of using these waters as medicine. Even though the water absorbed the flavor of these fruits, they are still forbidden because of the uncovered-liquids prohibition (see Tosefta ki-Fshuta, Terumot p. 413).
sharp. Pungent.
like apsintin. Wine mixed with wormwood. [Note: some read "apsintin"; so too in the Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 30a, and it is a Greek word and in Arabic too it is called by this name.]
and the same applies to other beverages. Into which something sharp or bitter was mixed.
the reptile. The snake.
the handle of a vessel. A vessel's handle, beneath which is the nearest place where a snake could hide.
but if the water was abundant enough that the bitterness would be lost in it. A certain quantity that was known to suffice to nullify the venom a snake injects at one time (Rav Ovadiah, Terumot 8:5).
the poison. The snake's venom.
whether in the ground or in vessels. Whether the water stands in the ground (a pool of water and the like), or is in a vessel.
a flowing spring. Whose waters flow.
a jug. A pitcher.
in the field, a chest and a tower. Types of cabinets.

in its carrying case. The jug's carrier. In all these cases we are concerned that a snake may have been in them beforehand without being noticed, or that they have a hole through which it could enter.
in a cistern, even a hundred cubits deep. Although the jug is deep in the ground, a snake could crawl there.
in a tower a hundred cubits high. A very tall structure, and a snake could climb to a height.

in a hall that is plastered and painted. A large room whose walls are painted and decorated, and one might have thought a snake would be deterred by the pictures on the wall (Chazon Yechezkel, Terumot 7:20, Tosefta ki-Fshuta, there p. 417).
if he checked the chest or the tower and then put it in, it is permitted. He checked that there is no snake in them and no hole.
a child's little finger. A baby's pinky, meaning a newborn infant (Kesef Mishneh).
he should not drink the tenth. For the venom does not mix throughout all the water, and there is a concern that it is concentrated in the water remaining in the barrel.
the venom of crawling creatures. Their poison.
that rises and floats above. It floats on the surface of the beverage.
even if he strained it through a strainer. For the venom passes through the holes of the strainer.
and he should not sprinkle the house with them. He should not wet the floor so the dust settles, lest the venom enter the feet of a person walking there barefoot.
and he should not knead clay with them. So that the venom does not enter the hands of the one kneading.
and he should not give an animal to drink from them. For if there is venom in them, it will kill the animal.
but he may give them to a cat to drink. For snake venom does not kill cats.
even if it is terumah, it is burned. Although it is forbidden to destroy dough of pure terumah (see also Hilchot Terumot 12:14).
and even if it was baked, the bread is forbidden. For the heat of baking does not nullify the force of the venom.
that ate a poison that kills a human. And if it ate a poison that kills an animal but not a human, it is permitted (Hilchot Shechitah 10:8).
before it changed in their bodies. Before it was digested.
until they are examined. Whether there is venom in their flesh.
if the flesh was not cut apart. For if there is venom in them, the flesh falls apart into pieces.
pecked figs etc.. Fruits or vegetables that were pierced by the bite of an animal.
even if he saw a bird or a mouse. Whose bite is not dangerous.
lest in the pecked place a hole was made. And a snake bit there before it.
whose stem was removed. An opening was made in the fruit at the place where it was picked from the tree, and likewise if it split naturally and not from being pecked.
they are not subject to the uncovered-liquids prohibition. Although it is possible that a snake pecked them at the open place, we are not that concerned.

therefore a person may eat figs and grapes at night without concern. Just as we are not concerned about pecking in a fig or grape whose stem was removed, so we are not concerned about pecking in other cases where no pecking is visible. Therefore it is permitted to eat at night even though he does not see whether there is pecking.
a pecked fig that dried and became a dried fig, and a pecked date that dried, both are permitted. For if there had been venom in them they would not have dried (Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 35a).
he spread his hand under his armpit. His palm in the armpit.
lest he touched with his hand a leper or a harmful substance. And when he touches his armpit he will contaminate his body with his hand.
for hands are busy. And perhaps he touched something and does not remember.
even though he is occupied with the meal. And intends to eat it immediately.

and similarly one should not stick a knife into an etrog or a radish, lest a person fall on the blade and die. When he sticks the tip of the knife into the fruit, this causes the blade to face upward and not lie on its side, and it will injure whoever falls on it.
a leaning wall etc.. For all of these are liable to fall.

if he meets a gentile on the road, he should turn him to his right. He should stand so that the gentile is on his right side, so that he can easily strike first and kill the gentile if the gentile rises to kill him (Meiri, Avodah Zarah 25a).
a Jew should not be below with the gentile above. When going up, the Jew goes up before the gentile, and when going down, the gentile goes down before the Jew.
he should bend down. Crouch.
he should crush. Break.
asks him. The gentile.
he should lengthen the road for him. He should tell him he is going to a place farther than the place he actually intends to go.
"until I come to my lord at Seir". Thus Yaakov said to Esav when Esav asked to accompany him, although he did not intend to go to Seir but only to Sukkot (see Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 25b).
It is forbidden to take medicine from a gentile. To buy a remedy from him or receive medical treatment from him, out of concern that he will kill the patient.

unless they have despaired of his living. Perhaps he will be cured by him nonetheless. And because of the chance he will be saved, we are not concerned that the gentile will hasten his death (see Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 27b).
the heretic. A denier.
a poultice. A food that is chewed and placed on the skin for medicinal purposes.
and a bandage. A dressing containing ointment (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:13).
and if it was a dangerous wound. One that could develop into a danger to life.
and any wound for which the Shabbat is desecrated. See Hilchot Shabbat 2:5.
and it is permitted to consult a gentile doctor. It is permitted to consult him about the appropriate remedy or treatment for the patient.
and it is forbidden to get a haircut from them in a private domain. In a place where many people are not found, he is not afraid to kill him.
he made himself appear to the gentile as an important person. He posed before him as an important person.
It is forbidden to sell gentiles any weapons etc.. See also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 9:8-9.
and one does not sharpen weapons for them. Such as swords and spears and the like.
neck-irons. Used for binding prisoners by the neck.
shackles... iron chains. Used for torture and binding.
lumps of Indian iron. Masses of raw iron from India, whose iron is of excellent quality and is used to manufacture weapons.
shields. Protective devices.
to the army of the people of the province because they protect the Jews. For the province's army protects the Jews living in the province.
a bandit. An armed robber.
strengthens the hands of transgressors and causes them to stumble. For by selling weapons he enables the bandit to carry out his acts.
and similarly anyone who causes a blind person to stumble in a matter, and advises him with improper advice. One who gives bad advice to a person who does not understand the field (a "blind person").

for he strengthened the hands of transgressors, who are blind and do not see the way of truth because of their heart's desire. A transgressor captive to his desires is considered blind, and it is forbidden to strengthen or assist him in committing the transgression (for examples of this prohibition see for instance Hilchot Gezelah 5:1, Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 2:7).
and even to advise him to do a mitzvah while he remains in his wickedness is forbidden. So as not to increase his merits.
and Daniel was not tested. He was punished by being thrown into the lions' den or by being brought down from his greatness (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 4a).

"therefore, O king, may my counsel be acceptable to you". The continuation of the verse: "and redeem your sins by charity and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; perhaps there will be a lengthening of your tranquility." Nevuchadnetzar feared the fulfillment of his bad dream, and Daniel gave him advice to give charity.
who encountered. Who met.
lying under its burden. Collapsed with the load because of its weight.
a load suitable for it. That it is ordinarily able to carry.
flustered. Confused and helpless.
he should help him up and then reload his burden on it. He should help him stand the animal up and load the cargo back on it in a way that it will not fall again.

and did not unload or load, he has neglected a positive commandment. Of unloading, but he did not neglect the commandment of loading, since before the unloading he was not yet obligated in it (Chatam Sofer on the 14 mitzvot, cited in Yad Pshutah; but in the view of Aruch ha-Shulchan, Choshen Mishpat 272:3, he also transgresses the positive commandment of loading).
if he was a kohen and the animal was lying in a cemetery. A kohen is forbidden to become impure with corpse impurity (Hilchot Avel 3:1-4), and one who enters a cemetery becomes impure.
just as he does not become impure to return a lost object. When he sees a lost object in a cemetery (Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 11:18).
an elder... and it is not according to his dignity, he is exempt. And the same law applies to a lost object (there, halachah 13).
this is the rule etc.. By this principle it is determined whether he is obligated to unload and load or exempt because of his dignity.
and if he was a pious person he does beyond the letter of the law. If he was a pious person whose practice is to go beyond the letter of the law.
he unloads and loads with him. Although he is exempt by the basic law (and the same applies to a lost object, Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 11:17).
"you shall surely help... you shall surely lift". From the form of the Hebrew verb, which repeats the verb, we learn that one must do so even many times (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 2:10).
to walk with him for a parsah. To accompany him along with the animal for a distance of a parsah (almost four kilometers) to make sure the animal does not collapse again.
from when is he obligated to unload and load with him. From what distance is he obligated to approach him to unload and load.
sight. From a distance.
which is like encountering. Which is considered an encounter, meaning sight from a close place.
one of seven and a half in a mil. A mil is two thousand cubits.
if he was farther from him than this, he need not attend to him. He is not obligated to approach and help him.
but to load it, this is a mitzvah and he takes his payment. Loading is a mitzvah and one is obligated to do it if the animal's owner needs it and wants it, but he may demand payment for it.
and similarly during the time he walks with him for a parsah he has payment. For the time he devotes to him.
in any case. In all circumstances.
and went and sat down. Without helping the unloader.
and if the animal's owner was elderly or ill. So that he is unable to unload with him.

if the gentile was driving his animal, he need not attend to it. The Jew's load is not damaged by the animal's collapse, and since the gentile is the one obligated to unload and load, he is exempt from unloading and loading. For this mitzvah applies toward another Jew and not toward a gentile.
driving. Leading the animal.
and if not. If the gentile is not driving his animal, and the Jew is responsible for looking after his load.

but as for the gentile's animal and its load, he is not obligated to deal with them except because of enmity. There is no obligation to unload and load, except in a case where his refusal to help would arouse hatred; but where it would not arouse hatred he is exempt.
donkey drivers. Those who lead donkeys.
whose legs are unsteady. And he cannot proceed quickly with his donkey.
his companions may not go ahead and pass him. Overtake him and leave him alone.
if the man fell. And cannot advance at all.
if one was loaded and one was riding. One donkey carries a load and a person rides the other donkey, and both wanted to pass through a narrow place where only one can pass.
they move the rider aside for the loaded one. They move and displace the rider from the road to allow the loaded one to pass first.
empty. Without cargo and without a rider.
they make a compromise between them. One passes first and pays the other for the loss he incurs from waiting (below, halachah 12).
and they meet each other; if both passed at once they would sink etc.. That they meet at a short distance in a strait that allows passage for only one boat.
on a high ascent and they met; if both passed at once they would fall. A narrow path on a mountain slope with no room for two camels to pass together.
near and far. One of the boats or one of the camels has a longer way to the destination it needs to reach.
since all of them are in equal urgency. The urgency of all of them to pass is the same.
impose a compromise between them, and they pay each other a fee. For if there is some loss to those waiting, those who went ahead compensate them.
"you shall judge with righteousness". A judgment that is a compromise (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 32b).
one who meets two, one with an animal lying down etc.. One needs help unloading his animal's burden, and the other needs help loading the burden on his animal.

it is a mitzvah to unload first, because of the suffering of living creatures. When he unloads the animal lying under its burden, he removes and prevents suffering for it in addition to the help he gives its owner.
both of them. The owners of the two animals.
if one was an enemy. There was hatred between the one who came to unload and load and the owner of the animal that needs loading.

it is a mitzvah to load with the enemy first, in order to subdue one's evil inclination. For a person has a natural feeling to help only his friends and not his enemies; against this the Torah commands that one help even his enemy, and not only that but that he give him priority over his friend, in order to subdue this feeling.
the enemy mentioned in the Torah. In the mitzvah of unloading: "When you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden" (Exodus 23:5).
he is a Jew, not one of the nations of the world. For there is no mitzvah to unload their animals (above, halachah 9).
and how can a Jew have an enemy among Jews, when the verse says, "You shall not hate your brother in your heart". See Hilchot De'ot 6:5.

who saw him alone. Without another witness who could join him in testimony (for if there is another witness they can testify about his deeds in court, and then everyone must hate him and he does not fall into the category of "one who hates you," Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 113b).

and he should not leave him on the verge of death, lest he be delayed on account of his money and come into danger. A person who is delayed on the road because of his money may reach a life-threatening situation from the dangers found on the road, and therefore leaving him there is treated as abandoning a person in mortal danger ("on the verge of death").

and the Torah was concerned about the lives of Jews, even among the wicked etc.. Although a person commits transgressions, if he does not deny the fundamentals of faith and does not intend to rebel or to spite, one must protect his life and take care not to endanger him (see above 4:10-12).
fourteen. Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 272:11.

it is a mitzvah to hate him until he repents and returns from his wickedness. The Shulchan Aruch copied the Rambam's words, and from their words it appears that although there is a mitzvah to hate him, nevertheless one must give him priority over others in order to subdue one's inclination. For this hatred stirs up other, forbidden hatreds between them (Bach in the name of Tosafot, Pesachim 113b; and see Tanya chapter 32, who wrote that although one must hate the evil in him, one must also love the good in him). In the view of the Rema (section 10), the obligation to give priority to the enemy applies to an ordinary enemy, but if he hates him because he committed a transgression there is no obligation to give him priority to subdue one's inclination, since he does well to hate him (though the mitzvah to help him unload and load still applies).
